about: The Daily's 'I never knew that' pool. Every entry carries the source's name, a link a reader can open, the date the source was read, and the source's own words the fact rests on. An entry without them is never shown (scripts/daily_fact.py, test/daily-email-v2.test.mjs). The old quote pool (data/quote-pool.json) stays off.

facts.fact: The biggest hailstone ever recovered in the US fell at Vivian, South Dakota, on June 23, 2010: 8 inches across and 1 lb 15 oz.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Hail
facts.quote: The largest hailstone recovered in the United States fell in Vivian, South Dakota, on June 23, 2010, with a diameter of 8 inches and a circumference of 18.62 inches. It weighed 1 lb 15 oz.

facts.fact: Hailstones bigger than 4 inches across can fall at over 100 mph. Hail under an inch falls at 9 to 25 mph.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Hail
facts.quote: For small hailstones (<1-inch in diameter), the expected fall speed is between 9 and 25 mph. ... it is possible for very large hailstones (diameters exceeding 4-inches) to fall at over 100 mph.

facts.fact: 2 corn kernels on every square foot behind the combine add up to a bushel an acre left in the field.
facts.source: Iowa State University Integrated Crop Management (Hanna, 2010)
facts.quote: Two corn kernels per square foot or a single three-quarter pound ear in 436 square feet (0.01 acre) equals one bushel per acre of corn loss

facts.fact: One dropped ear in a 20 by 22 foot patch behind an 8-row head is a bushel an acre lost.
facts.source: Iowa State University Integrated Crop Management (Hanna, 2010)
facts.quote: Finding just one ear by kicking through residue in a 20 x 22 foot area behind an 8-row cornhead equals one bushel per acre loss.

facts.fact: Over half of corn harvest losses happen at the cornhead, where the combine's loss sensors cannot see them.
facts.source: Iowa State University Integrated Crop Management (Hanna, 2010)
facts.quote: Over half of corn harvest losses occur at the cornhead and are not able to be measured by grain loss sensors on the rear of the combine.

facts.fact: 4 to 5 soybeans on the ground per square foot add up to a bushel an acre lost.
facts.source: Nebraska Extension CropWatch: Harvest soybeans at 13% moisture
facts.quote: Four to five beans on the ground per square foot can add up to one bushel per acre loss.

facts.fact: Corn at 20% moisture is like five rail cars of grain where one whole car is water.
facts.source: Purdue University Corny News (Nielsen): grain moisture and water shrink
facts.quote: if the grain moisture content was 20%, that would be equivalent to four grain cars of absolute dry matter and one grain car of water

facts.fact: There were 94.2 million cattle and calves on US farms on July 1, 2026. The 2026 calf crop was put at 32.5 million head, down 2% from 2025.
facts.source: USDA NASS, July 2026 Cattle report news release
facts.quote: There were 94.2 million head of cattle and calves on U.S. farms as of July 1, 2026 ... U.S. calf crop was estimated at 32.5 million head, down 2% from 2025.

facts.fact: The US had 28.5 million beef cows on July 1, 2026, down 1% from a year earlier.
facts.source: USDA NASS, July 2026 Cattle report news release
facts.quote: There are 28.5 million beef cows in the United States as of July 1, 2026, down 1% from last year.

facts.fact: The 2026 national average marketing loan rate is $2.42 a bushel for corn and $6.82 for soybeans.
facts.source: USDA FSA, 2026 National Average Loan Rates
facts.quote: Corn $2.42 per bushel ... Soybeans $6.82 per bushel

facts.fact: Flat storage holds about 0.8 bushel for every cubic foot of grain: length times width times depth times 0.8.
facts.source: Nebraska Extension CropWatch: How to estimate bushels in a grain bin
facts.quote: For rectangular flat storage buildings, the math is simpler. Multiply length (ft) by width (ft) by grain depth (ft) by 0.8 bushels per cubic foot.

facts.fact: The 'normal' rain on a weather page is a 30-year average that NOAA redoes every 10 years. Today's normals cover 1991 to 2020.
facts.source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals
facts.quote: NCEI generates the official U.S. normals every 10 years ... The 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals are the latest in a series of decadal normals first produced in the 1950s.
